content: Tamoxifen is a critical medication used in the treatment of breast cancer. Ovarian cancer cells are known to express hormone receptors, which suggests that they may also respond to tamoxifen therapy. Tamoxifen is specifically utilized in women with breast cancer whose tumors express estrogen receptors. Since ovarian cancers frequently exhibit estrogen receptors as well, it has been hypothesized that tamoxifen could provide therapeutic benefits in this context. The purpose of this review was to evaluate the effects of tamoxifen in women with relapsed ovarian cancer. To conduct this review, a comprehensive search was performed across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), the Cochrane Gynaecological Cancer Group Trials Register, MEDLINE (from 2002 to April 2009), and EMBASE (from 2002 to April 2009). Additional sources such as clinical trial registries, abstracts from scientific meetings, reference lists of review articles, and consultations with field experts and pharmaceutical companies were also utilized. The inclusion criteria for this review were randomized and non-randomized studies involving women with ovarian cancer who had not responded to standard chemotherapy. Only studies with a sample size of 10 or more patients were considered eligible. Two independent reviewers assessed the identified studies to determine whether they met the inclusion criteria. The search process yielded 1,392 unique references. Of these, 1,360 were excluded based on their titles and abstracts. The remaining 32 articles were reviewed in full, but none met the inclusion criteria for this analysis. Consequently, no randomized or comparative trials were identified, and no data were available for analysis. The only available evidence came from observational, single-arm studies involving women treated with tamoxifen. The authors concluded that no evidence-based recommendations could be made regarding the use of tamoxifen in women with recurrent ovarian cancer due to the lack of comparative studies. While limited evidence from phase 2 studies suggests some anti-tumor activity of tamoxifen, there is no data available on its impact on symptom control, quality of life, or survival outcomes.
